s0201.literal: Moreover he dedicated himself solely to writing books; white-haired yet unwearying, he copied with his own hand and never paused for a moment.
s0201.idiomatic: Moreover he devoted himself solely to writing; though white-haired he never tired, copying with his own hand and never pausing.

s0202.literal: He especially loved examining ancient and modern texts and correcting written forms; his brilliance flowed richly, and though old he did not fade.
s0202.idiomatic: He especially loved scrutinizing past and present texts and correcting written forms; his brilliance remained rich, and age did not dull it.

s0203.literal: He was also versed in Buddhist scriptures; essays he wrote on temples, stupas, and many monks were especially refined and dense.
s0203.idiomatic: He was also versed in Buddhist scriptures; his writings on temples, stupas, and monks were especially refined.

s0204.literal: In office he recommended many; any merit that could be recorded he always rewarded and advanced.
s0204.idiomatic: In office he recommended many; any merit worth recording he rewarded and advanced.

s0205.literal: If someone importuned him beyond his station, he all sent them away according to reason.
s0205.idiomatic: Anyone who importuned him beyond his station he dismissed on principle.

s0206.literal: He served the sovereign with utmost loyalty, doing whatever he knew should be done.
s0206.idiomatic: He served the sovereign wholeheartedly and did whatever he knew should be done.

s0207.literal: In handling confidential matters he never leaked.
s0207.idiomatic: In confidential service he never leaked a word.

s0208.literal: Moreover his appointments had grown lofty and he belonged to the upper ranks; he deeply wished to withdraw and be quiet, avoiding sound and power.
s0208.idiomatic: His appointments had grown lofty and he stood among the foremost; he deeply wished to withdraw, avoiding fame and power.

s0209.literal: Pure and clean in his conduct, his property was always depleted; when some urged him to plan for livelihood he only smiled and did not answer.
s0209.idiomatic: Pure in conduct, his property was always bare; when some urged him to plan for livelihood he only smiled and said nothing.

s0210.literal: Gentle to kinsmen, steadfast to old friends; all salary and gifts he gave wholly to relieve those around him.
s0210.idiomatic: Gentle to kin and steadfast to old friends, he gave all salary and gifts to support those around him.

s0211.literal: Houzhu's literary drafts were numerous in scrolls; he had a separate copy made and given to Cha; whenever in doubt he had him revise and fix; Cha also served with open heart, nothing hidden.
s0211.idiomatic: Houzhu's literary drafts filled many scrolls; he had a separate copy made for Cha and had him revise whatever was doubtful; Cha served with an open heart and hid nothing.

s0212.literal: Houzhu once said leisurely to court gentlemen: "Yao Cha's learning is penetrating and his knowledge broad, his brush's literary measure; seeking in antiquity [12] he is hard to match as an equal; in the present age he suffices as a model.
s0212.idiomatic: Houzhu once told court gentlemen at ease, "Yao Cha's learning is deep and his knowledge wide, and his writing sets the literary standard; [12] few in antiquity equal him, and in our age he is a model.

s0213.literal: Moreover his responses are very detailed and clear [13]; hearing them makes one forget weariness.
s0213.idiomatic: His answers are [13] very detailed and clear; to hear them is to forget weariness.

s0214.literal: " Whenever Cha composed a literary draft, an edict at once demanded the original; the sovereign said: "I toward Yao Cha's essays [14] not only savor them without end—he is truly a patriarch of the craft."
s0214.idiomatic: " Whenever Cha wrote, the court at once demanded the draft; the sovereign said, "[14] I never tire of savoring Yao Cha's essays—he is truly a master of the craft."

s0215.literal: Xu Ling's name towered for a generation; whenever he saw Cha's compositions he especially prized them.
s0215.idiomatic: Xu Ling's name stood at the height of his age; whenever he saw Cha's compositions he prized them especially.

s0216.literal: He once told his son Jian: "Academician Yao's virtue and learning have no precedent—you may take him as teacher."
s0216.idiomatic: He once told his son Jian, "Academician Yao's virtue and learning have no precedent—you should take him as your teacher."

s0217.literal: Director of the Masters of Writing Jiang Zong was especially thick friends with Cha; whenever he had a composition he always first sent a note to Cha, then put it into use.
s0217.idiomatic: Jiang Zong, director of the masters of writing, was especially close to Cha; whenever he wrote something he first sent it to Cha, then published it.

s0218.literal: When Zong was junior mentor he once composed a five-hundred-character poem on ascending the palace wall; at the time the heir apparent and Xu Ling and other famous scholars all joined in the same composition.
s0218.idiomatic: When Zong was junior mentor he wrote a five-hundred-character poem on climbing the palace wall; the heir apparent, Xu Ling, and other famous scholars all wrote matching pieces.

s0219.literal: Master Xu later told Jiang: "My fifty-rhyme response to my younger brother is in my brother's collection."
s0219.idiomatic: Xu later told Jiang, "My fifty-rhyme response to my younger brother is in my brother's collection."

s0220.literal: When Jiang arranged his writings he could no longer find Cha's matching piece; stating Xu's meaning, he told Cha: "With lofty talent and great learning you might glorify my poor piece; now I need your five hundred characters to pair with Master Xu's chapter."
s0220.idiomatic: When Jiang edited his writings he could not find Cha's matching poem; repeating Xu's request, he told Cha, "With your great talent you might glorify my poor piece; I need your five hundred characters to pair with Master Xu's chapter."

s0221.literal: Cha modestly did not deliver it; Jiang said: "If I cannot obtain your piece, my poem too must be discarded, and again I fail what Master Xu entrusted—how can both be lost at once?"
s0221.idiomatic: Cha modestly withheld it; Jiang said, "Without your piece I must discard my poem too and again fail what Master Xu entrusted—how can both be lost?"

s0222.literal: Cha, unable to refuse further, then copied out the piece and gave it to him.
s0222.idiomatic: Unable to refuse further, Cha copied out the piece and gave it to him.

s0223.literal: Esteemed by men of discernment—every case was like this.
s0223.idiomatic: Esteemed by men of discernment—every case was like this.

s0224.literal: His writings include Exegesis and Digest of the Han History in thirty scrolls, Forest of Discourses in ten scrolls, Western Embassy Memorial, Jade Seal Memorial, and Record of the Three Bells of Jiankang, each one scroll—all exhaustively broad—and collected works in twenty scrolls, all circulating in the world.
s0224.idiomatic: He wrote Exegesis and Digest of the Han History in thirty scrolls, Forest of Discourses in ten scrolls, and one scroll each on the western embassy, the jade seal, and the three bells of Jiankang—all exhaustively learned—plus collected works in twenty scrolls, all in circulation.

s0225.literal: Though Cha's Liang and Chen histories were not finished, in Emperor Wen of Sui's Kaihuang era the court sent Secretariat Aide Yu Shiji to demand the draft and it was submitted; it is now in the inner palace.
s0225.idiomatic: Though Cha's Liang and Chen histories were unfinished, in Sui Wendi's Kaihuang era the court sent secretariat aide Yu Shiji to demand the draft and receive it; it is now in the inner palace.

s0226.literal: The Liang and Chen histories were mostly Cha's composition; prefaces, discussions, annals, and biographies had gaps; on the verge of death he still charged his son Sijian with the format and rules, to seek widely and continue writing; Sijian wept and carried it out.
s0226.idiomatic: The Liang and Chen histories were mostly Cha's work; prefaces, discussions, annals, and biographies still had gaps. On his deathbed he charged his son Sijian with the format and rules to seek sources and continue the work; Sijian wept and obeyed.

s0227.literal: Sijian in Chen was recorder in the Hengyang prince's household, then registrar to the prince of Kuaiji.
s0227.idiomatic: In Chen, Sijian was recorder in the Hengyang prince's household, then registrar to the prince of Kuaiji.

s0228.literal: Entering Sui he was made staff aide to the Prince of Han and director of the secretariat office; soon he was made judicial administrator of Hejian commandery.
s0228.idiomatic: Entering Sui he became staff aide to the prince of Han and director of the secretariat office, then judicial administrator of Hejian commandery.

s0229.literal: At the opening of Daye, Secretariat Vice Director Yu Shiji memorialized that Sijian should follow and complete the Liang and Chen histories; from then the work gradually was supplemented.
s0229.idiomatic: At the opening of Daye, secretariat vice director Yu Shiji memorialized that Sijian should follow and complete the Liang and Chen histories; from then the work was gradually supplemented.

s0231.literal: The historiographer says: Jiang Zong held a clear emblem, simple and noble, adorned with literary color; when he headed the six ministries he fully matched court hopes.
s0231.idiomatic: The historiographer says: Jiang Zong bore a clear emblem, simple and noble, adorned with literary grace; when he headed the six ministries he fully matched what the court hoped for.

s0232.literal: The historiographer's late father received these fine virtues [15], illuminating these hundred conduct—he could reform customs and thicken human relations.
s0232.idiomatic: The historiographer's late father possessed these fine virtues [15] and lit up every side of conduct—he could reform custom and thicken human relations.

s0233.literal: As for books of the nine streams and seven summaries, records of famous mountains and stone chambers, books from the Ji commandery and Kong family hall, texts of jade cases and gold boards—none escaped deep study of their purport or full probing of their depths; therefore he led the way as teacher of men, and gentry took him as their standard.
s0233.idiomatic: Books of the nine streams and seven summaries, records from famous mountains and stone chambers, texts from the Ji cache and Kong hall, writings on jade cases and gold boards—none escaped deep study or full probing; he led the way as a teacher of men, and the gentry took him as their standard.

s0234.literal: Having served in lofty posts, on state canons and court regulations and ancient and modern doubtful points Houzhu all took my late father's judgment.
s0234.idiomatic: After he rose to lofty posts, on state canons, court regulations, and ancient and modern doubtful points Houzhu always took my late father's judgment.

s0236.literal: [1] Uncle Marquis of Pingguang Wu Xiao Mo—"Mo" in the Book of Liang biography of Xiao Jing and the Southern History biography of Marquis of Wu Pingguang Jing both read "Li"; the Southern History biography of Jiang Zong again reads "Mo."
s0236.idiomatic: On "uncle Marquis of Pingguang Wu Xiao Mo": the Book of Liang biography of Xiao Jing and the Southern History biography of Marquis of Wu Pingguang Jing read Li for Mo; the Southern History biography of Jiang Zong again reads Mo.

s0237.literal: According to Gui Fu's Exegesis of Meaning in the Shuowen, the character "Mo" may also be written "Li."
s0237.idiomatic: Gui Fu's Exegesis of Meaning in the Shuowen says Mo may also be written Li.

s0238.literal: [2] The marquis's great-grandfather, Jin protector-general of the army
s0238.idiomatic: [2] The marquis's great-grandfather, Jin protector-general of the army

s0240.literal: [Biao]—According to Jiang Biao's biography in the Jin History he was the son of Jiang Tong and once served as protector-general; now changed accordingly.
s0240.idiomatic: On "[Biao]": Jiang Biao has a biography in the Jin History; he was Jiang Tong's son and once served as protector-general; now emended accordingly.

s0243.literal: [stone] character—the Hall edition's textual verification says the character "at" is suspected as an error.
s0243.idiomatic: On "[stone] character": the Hall edition suspects at is wrong.

s0244.literal: Comment: this uses the First Emperor's ascent of Kuaiji Mountain and erecting a stone inscription praising Qin virtue—"at" should be "stone," a form-similar corruption.
s0244.idiomatic: This refers to the First Emperor's ascent of Mount Kuaiji and a stone inscription praising Qin; at should be stone, a form-similar error.

s0245.literal: Wenyuan yinghua 97 correctly reads "stone"; the Jinling edition already changed it to stone; now followed.
s0245.idiomatic: Wenyuan yinghua 97 reads stone; the Jinling edition already has stone; now followed.

s0246.literal: [4] Rain makes the forest sing while wind whistles elegantly—"elegant" is suspected as a corruption; Fu Zengxiang collated Wenyuan yinghua, changing per the Song edition to "whistling."
s0246.idiomatic: On "rain makes the forest sing while wind whistles elegantly": elegant is probably corrupt; Fu Zengxiang collated Wenyuan yinghua and, following the Song edition, reads whistling.

s0247.literal: [5] With Chen Xuan, Kong Fan, Wang
s0247.idiomatic: [5] With Chen Xuan, Kong Fan, Wang

s0249.literal: [Wang] and more than ten men—changed according to the Southern History and Comprehensive Mirror, Chen Changcheng Gong Zhide year 2.
s0249.idiomatic: On "[Wang] and more than ten men": emended per the Southern History and Comprehensive Mirror, Chen Changcheng Gong Zhide year 2.

s0250.literal: [6] Father Director-General of the Upper Secretariat Monk
s0250.idiomatic: [6] Father Director-General of the Upper Secretariat Monk

s0252.literal: [Yuan]—According to Yao Sengyuan's biography in the Zhou History, tan and yuan are form-similar corruptions; now changed accordingly.
s0252.idiomatic: On "[Yuan]": Yao Sengyuan has a biography in the Zhou History; tan and yuan are form-similar errors; now emended accordingly.

s0256.literal: [ku] mourning shed—changed according to the Southern Supervisory and Hall editions.
s0256.idiomatic: On "[ku] mourning shed": emended per the Southern Supervisory and Hall editions.

s0257.literal: [8] Then with divine brush he drafted the edict—the Hall edition's textual verification says "divine" is suspected as an error for "extend the brush."
s0257.idiomatic: On "then with divine brush he drafted the edict": the Hall edition suspects divine for extend the brush.

s0258.literal: Zhang Senkai's collation note says: "In antiquity there was extending the paper; extending the brush is unheard of—'divine' is correct."
s0258.idiomatic: Zhang Senkai's collation note says antiquity had extending the paper, not the brush—divine is correct.

s0259.literal: Present examination: the Literary Treatises sequence has the phrase "divine brush reward," and He Zhiyuan's biography also has "divine brush edict"; the author of the verification was utterly blind to these—extremely shallow and reckless.
s0259.idiomatic: Present examination: the Literary Treatises sequence has divine brush reward, and He Zhiyuan's biography has divine brush edict; the verifier ignored both—shallow and reckless.

s0260.literal: [9] Cha wept and bowed, saying, "I, eastern Gao low clan"—the two characters "said I" were originally ink dots in the base text and are now supplied from the various editions.
s0260.idiomatic: On "Cha wept and bowed, saying, I, eastern Gao low clan": said I were ink dots in the base text and are restored from other editions.

s0261.literal: [10] One bolt of patterned silk—"silk" in all editions reads "practice silk."
s0261.idiomatic: On "one bolt of patterned silk": all editions read practice silk for silk.

s0262.literal: Comment: below it says "what I wear is only hemp cloth and rush silk"; rush silk pairs with patterned silk, so writing "silk" is correct; the Southern History correctly reads "silk."
s0262.idiomatic: Below he says he wears only hemp cloth and rush silk; rush silk pairs with patterned silk, so silk is correct; the Southern History agrees.

s0263.literal: [11] Cha sternly drove him out—"stern" in the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions reads "fierce."
s0263.idiomatic: On "Cha sternly drove him out": the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions read fierce for stern.

s0264.literal: Comment: stern and fierce are interchangeable.

s0265.literal: [12] Seeking in antiquity—the three characters "seeking in antiquity" were originally ink dots in the base text and are now supplied from Yuan Gui 192.
s0265.idiomatic: On "seeking in antiquity": the three words were ink dots in the base text and are restored from Yuan Gui 192.

s0266.literal: Comment: "seeking in antiquity" pairs with below "in the present age"; various editions read "exquisite since antiquity," which is probably wrong.
s0266.idiomatic: Seeking in antiquity pairs with in the present age below; various editions read exquisite since antiquity, which is probably wrong.

s0267.literal: [13] Moreover his responses are very detailed and clear—the three characters "very detailed and clear" were originally ink dots in the base text and are now supplied from the various editions.
s0267.idiomatic: On "moreover his responses are very detailed and clear": the three words were ink dots in the base text and are restored from other editions.

s0268.literal: [14] The sovereign said, "I toward Yao Cha's essays"—the characters "sovereign" and "toward" were originally ink dots in the base text and are now supplied from the various editions.
s0268.idiomatic: On "the sovereign said, I toward Yao Cha's essays": sovereign and toward were ink dots in the base text and are restored from other editions.

s0269.literal: [15] The historiographer's late father received these fine virtues—below "first" the character "minister" was originally an ink dot in the base text and is now supplied from the various editions.
s0269.idiomatic: On "the historiographer's late father received these fine virtues": below first, minister was an ink dot in the base text and is restored from other editions.
